//launcher: Commands go through run-hook.cmd rather than bare `node` on purpose. A hook that cannot find its interpreter fails SILENTLY: both hosts treat a non-zero hook exit as 'no decision' and carry on, so the guards look configured while enforcing nothing. The launcher resolves node defensively and, if it truly cannot, says so via systemMessage instead of exiting quietly.
//claude-prompt-hooks: `claudePromptHooks` below is CLAUDE-ONLY and is merged into .claude/settings.json by the sync. Copilot reads `hooks` and ignores this key. A `type: "prompt"` hook is a different mechanism from the `type: "command"` hooks in `hooks`: the host spawns NO process. BOTH reasons Claude registers no command hooks here are therefore void -- there is no `cmd /c`, so no console window to flash (#91264) and nothing that can hang holding one open -- and they were measured to FIRE ON AN UNTRUSTED WORKSPACE, unlike permissions.allow. See CONTROL-PLANE-NOTES.md section 11.
//claude-prompt-hooks-are-conditions: READ THIS BEFORE EDITING A PROMPT BELOW. A prompt hook is NOT a judge that returns JSON. It is a CONDITION EVALUATOR, the same machinery as `/goal`. The host treats your `prompt` as a statement that must be TRUE for the turn to be allowed to end, hands it to a model along with the turn, and gets back prose. When the condition is judged unmet the host injects `Stop hook feedback:\n[<your prompt verbatim>]: <the evaluator's reasoning>` into the conversation and the turn continues. Consequence, learned the expensive way: a prompt phrased as an INSTRUCTION -- 'respond {"ok": true} unless...' -- is read as a requirement that the assistant emit that JSON. It never does, so the condition is never satisfied and the hook BLOCKS EVERY TURN FOREVER. An earlier revision of this file shipped exactly that. Phrase every prompt as a condition about work already done, and say explicitly which turns satisfy it trivially. Verified 2026-09-18 on 2.1.211: the corrected Stop condition below passes a clean turn in num_turns:1 and blocks an unevidenced `all quality gates pass` claim, citing its own rule 1.
//claude-prompt-hooks-cost: MEASURED, not assumed. The evaluator runs on the MAIN model (claude-opus-4-8 in the probe), not a small one, and a Stop hook costs about +$0.042 per turn -- two independent trivial-turn samples went $0.0647 -> $0.1069 and $0.0468 -> $0.0887, a consistent +$0.042 and roughly +1.7x on a cheap turn. That is genuinely cheap only in the dimension that killed the command hooks (no subprocess, no console flash); it is NOT free. Both entries below are therefore deliberately LOW-FREQUENCY: Stop fires once per turn, SubagentStop only when the reviewer finishes. A PreToolUse prompt hook on Bash|PowerShell was considered and REJECTED -- it would fire on the highest-frequency tool in this workflow, and the deny list already covers the destructive cases synchronously and for free. Keep that bar: each hook here must map to a failure that actually happened in this repo. To opt out entirely, delete the entry and re-run `pnpm agents:sync`.

Stop.//: TWO conditions in one hook, because a second prompt hook would double the per-turn cost for no gain. PART A is the Evidence Requirement: gate 7 was once reported green while Playwright was exiting 1 -- a backgrounded `| tail` printed the WRAPPER's `[exited with code 0]` while the inner run printed `[ELIFECYCLE] Command failed with exit code 1`. Prose in quality-gates.instructions.md did not prevent that; nothing read it at the moment it mattered. This does. PART B is the No-Pause rule from agentic-workflow.instructions.md, added 2026-09-19 under the owner's autonomy mandate -- that rule had existed only as prose, and prose does not fire at the moment a turn ends with 'want me to continue?'. Note the two parts have SEPARATE escape clauses on purpose: Part A's 'no gate claims were made' escape must NOT reach Part B, or the no-pause rule would be nullified on exactly the turns that pause without running a gate.
Stop.prompt:
This turn satisfies the repository's evidence rule and its no-pause rule. Both parts below must hold; each carries its own scope, and neither escape clause applies to the other part.

== PART A: evidence for gate claims ==

Satisfied when all of the following hold for the assistant's work in this turn:

1. Every quality gate the assistant claimed to have passed -- format, lint, types/tsc, test, coverage, build, e2e, audit, bundle, or SSR/no-JS -- has that gate's verbatim command output present in the transcript. Real evidence looks like `Tests  339 passed (339)`, `47 passed (2.1m)`, `Compiled successfully`, `found 0 vulnerabilities`. A bare assertion such as "lint is clean" or "all gates pass" with no output does not satisfy this.
2. Any gate left red, or any command that failed, was stated plainly rather than omitted or glossed.
3. No test was skipped, deleted, or loosened to get green; no coverage threshold in vitest.config.mts was lowered; no coverage exclusion was added to make a number pass; `--no-verify` was not used.
4. Any piped command whose success was asserted was judged by `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` rather than `$?` -- after a pipeline `$?` is the last stage's status, usually sed's, and is almost always 0.
5. Any claim that gate 7 / Playwright passed was preceded by confirming port 3000 was free, because `reuseExistingServer` otherwise silently tests an already-running server and can report a false green.

ESCAPE CLAUSE FOR PART A ONLY: a turn that made no quality-gate claims at all -- research, explanation, planning, answering a question, or editing files without asserting a gate result -- satisfies PART A automatically. Part A is a check on claims the assistant actually made; it is NOT an instruction to produce any particular output, and must never be read as requiring the assistant to run a gate it was not asked to run.

== PART B: the work was carried as far as it could go ==

Satisfied when EITHER of the following holds -- this is a disjunction, and meeting either one is enough:

6a. The turn did not end by asking the user for permission, confirmation, or a go-ahead to continue work the user had already asked for. Reporting finished work, stating a result, asking nothing, or handing back a completed deliverable all satisfy this.

OR

6b. The turn did end with a question or a pause, and the reason is one the repository sanctions: missing credentials or a missing secret; a destructive or irreversible action awaiting approval; publishing -- `git push`, opening a PR, deploying, sending mail; genuinely ambiguous requirements where two readings produce incompatible work; the review round cap (round 5) being reached; a planner Level 4 classification; a guard or permission rule blocking work the task genuinely requires; an architectural choice with no precedent in the codebase; or the user's own explicit instruction to stop and check in. A question that is merely offering optional follow-up work, alongside a completed deliverable, also satisfies this.

IMPORTANT, and this is what Part B is for: "I have finished step one, shall I proceed to step two?" on work the user already requested does NOT satisfy Part B. Neither does presenting findings and waiting for permission to act on them, nor asking whether to delegate to a subagent. The repository's pipeline is automatic by design.

Part B is NOT a demand that the assistant keep working indefinitely, never ask a clarifying question, or never hand control back. A turn that finished what was asked and stopped is fully satisfying. So is a turn that stopped for any reason in 6b.

SubagentStop.//: Guards both directions of the reviewer's verdict: an unsupported GREEN (the dangerous one) and a padded RED (the expensive one). agentic-workflow.instructions.md says a reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some even when the work is sound, and that each false RED costs a full round.
SubagentStop.//do-not-delete-the-escape-clause: The first paragraph of the prompt looks redundant next to `matcher` below. It is not, and on this binary it is the difference between a guard and an outage. CHANGELOG 2.1.2xx: 'Fixed SubagentStop hooks with a specific matcher firing for every stopping subagent whose agent type was empty' -- that fix landed AFTER 2.1.211, which is what is installed here, so the matcher cannot be trusted to scope this hook. Without the escape clause a stray fire on a researcher is unsurvivable: rule 1 demands a `VERDICT:` line, a research report has never contained one, the condition can therefore never be satisfied, and that subagent is blocked forever -- the exact failure documented in CONTROL-PLANE-NOTES.md section 11.1, narrowed to one agent type. Every condition scoped by a matcher needs to restate its own scope in prose. Delete this clause only after verifying the installed binary is >= the version carrying that fix.
SubagentStop.prompt:
Either the stopping subagent is not the `reviewer`, or its report is well-formed.

FIRST, the escape clause, and it is load-bearing. This condition concerns the `reviewer` agent ONLY. If the subagent that just stopped is a researcher, implementer, scribe, debugger, planner, memory-updater, or anything else that does not produce a review verdict, the condition is SATISFIED AUTOMATICALLY and nothing below applies. Do not judge such a report against the rules that follow; they describe a document it was never supposed to write.

Otherwise -- the stopping subagent IS the reviewer -- the condition is satisfied when all of the following hold:

1. The report contains an explicit `VERDICT: GREEN` or `VERDICT: RED` line.
2. If the verdict is GREEN, the verbatim command output of each gate the report claims to have run appears in the report -- not a summary of it.
3. If the verdict is RED, at least one blocking finding names a CONCRETE failure: a specific input or state leading to a specific wrong output, crash, or violated gate. Findings that are only preferences -- "consider extracting this", "this could be more robust" -- are opinions and belong in a separate optional list that does not block GREEN. A RED made up solely of those does not satisfy this condition.

IMPORTANT: a clean diff returning GREEN on round 1 is the CORRECT outcome and satisfies this condition. Brevity is not a defect, and this condition must never be read as requiring the reviewer to find problems.
